title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) to measure whether interposing a deterministic network verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated device configurations that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one identical initial LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification) we evaluated 72 preregistered intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 72 baseline executions produced no emulator‑observed faults (n_11 = 72, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0). The paired difference in undetected‑fault proportion is 0.0 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Confirmatory interpretation: for the chosen model, task bank, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the verifier did not reduce undetected faults because none were observed in the baseline (a ceiling effect). We present preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, precise inferential outputs, and concrete limitations that motivate alternative designs (adversarial tasks, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model sampling) required to assess verifier utility under realistic error regimes.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate high‑level operator intent into low‑level device configurations and thus offer potential productivity gains for network operations (NetOps). Prior controlled studies report promising intent→configuration accuracy under constrained vendor dialects, while surveys and prototype systems stress the operational risks of semantic errors, incorrect command ordering, and protocol misuse that may cause outages or policy violations [1], [2]. A canonical mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that places deterministic validators (e.g., header‑space or policy checkers) between generation and execution to detect violations before changes are applied [3], [4]. However, direct, preregistered empirical evidence quantifying how much a verifier reduces executed, undetected faults on realistic task banks is limited. This study tests the narrowly framed research question that was preregistered before execution: Does coupling an LLM generator with a canonical deterministic network verifier materially reduce the proportion of LLM candidates that would execute with operational faults compared to executing the same candidate without verification when the identical candidate is evaluated under both conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics)?

Contributions. (1) We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (study id c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) with deterministic execution accounting and archived artifacts. (2) We provide exact, artifact‑grounded inferential outputs showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (no baseline faults) and explain the methodological implications. (3) We identify concrete follow‑on experimental designs that avoid ceiling effects and better reveal verifier utility.
sections.related_work: LLM‑based intent→configuration translation has been demonstrated in constrained settings and vendor dialects with measurable task accuracy [1]. Multi‑agent and tool‑augmented frameworks integrate validators and orchestration to reduce regressions in NetOps workflows; system prototypes illustrate possible integrations but lack standardized, preregistered end‑to‑end evaluation of verifier detection performance on execution outcomes [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures are widely proposed and empirically instantiated in code repair and regulated engineering domains to combine stochastic generation with deterministic checks [3]; however, available evidence adapting GVR specifically to network verifiers and reporting executed outcomes is limited. Classical network verification techniques such as header‑space analysis provide efficient reachability and policy checks and are natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks [4]. Our work contributes a narrowly scoped, preregistered empirical test that couples an LLM generator (gpt-5-mini) with a deterministic network verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and reports exact, archived emulator outcomes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the study (c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001) and froze hypotheses, sampling, and analysis code before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired reduction in undetected operational‑fault proportion: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory hypothesis H1 prespecified a two‑sided paired test to detect an absolute paired reduction of 0.20 with alpha = 0.05 and power >= 0.80; the registered sample size was N = 72 paired intents stratified across three topology complexity strata.

Design semantics and shared_initial_candidate constraint. Per the preregistered execution_contract, the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced one identical initial generation per intent (one model call) and that same candidate was evaluated under both baseline (execute) and guarded (verify‑then‑execute‑if‑not‑flagged) conditions. Under guarded, verifier flags render the outcome "prevented" without executing the candidate; otherwise the candidate is executed. The design isolates verifier detection performance on identical outputs and intentionally avoids conflating generator‑variation effects.

Model, adapter, and verifier. All initial generations declared requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic verifier used was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; verifier traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validator_version, validation_before and validation_after states for each episode (examples archived in execution/scoring/*.json). The recorded model configuration shows sampling fields unset (temperature = null); the recorded artifact is authoritative and indicates provider defaults determined runtime sampling behavior (this residual uncertainty is documented in the archived model_configuration.json).

Task bank, constraints, and contamination checks. Tasks were drawn from a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest entry includes: explicit intent, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, difficulty metadata (level and pattern), and expected_final_state. Per preregistration, exact‑match contamination checks against public corpora were applied; exact matches would be excluded from confirmatory analysis. In the executed run no confirmatory pairs were excluded.

Execution, retries, and missingness. The preregistered missingness_plan allowed up to two transient retries for hosted‑API errors. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 144 (72 pairs × 2 conditions), completed_model_calls = 72 (one shared initial generation per pair), and failed_episode_count = 0. All provider call counts, stage counts, and cache metrics are archived in deterministic_reconciliation.json and provider_call_audit.

Scoring and primary analysis. Validator scoring used the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with rule full_intent_constraint_validation; each episode records a binary score (valid configuration vs. violation) and detailed validator_trace. The primary analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency table and ran an exact McNemar two‑sided test when applicable; bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (seed 1729) for descriptive rates. All analysis scripts, the paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv are archived and hashed.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifact consistency. The preregistered run completed without technical failures. Key deterministic counts from archived artifacts: planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 72; complete_pair_count = 72. The provider_call_audit reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 72, cache_miss_count = 72, and single stage shared_initial_generation = 72.

Primary contingency and inferential outputs. The paired contingency table aggregated across 72 pairs is: n_11 = 72 (baseline succeeded and guarded succeeded), n_10 = 0 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n_01 = 0 (guarded failed, baseline succeeded), n_00 = 0 (both failed). The estimated paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples; seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. The condition summaries in archived analysis/condition_summary.csv record baseline success_rate = 1.0 and guarded success_rate = 1.0.

Representative validator traces. Representative execution/scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-00000{1..6}-*.json) show that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parsed commands and validated intent constraints for every shared candidate. Example metadata present in traces: parsed_command_count, required_command_count, difficulty.level (medium/hard/very_hard), normalized_configuration, validation_before and validation_after states, validator_version = "5.0", and score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION" for these examples. The traces confirm that the verifier ran on all shared candidates and that no verifier flags led to emulator‑observed faults in this sample.

Interpretation of numeric results. The inferential outputs are degenerate because there was no variation across pairs: the bootstrap CI collapsed to a single point and the exact test reports no evidence of a difference (p = 1.0). This outcome is internally consistent and precisely reflects the preregistered estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics: the verifier cannot reduce undetected executed faults if none occurred in the baseline executions of the identical candidates.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation and ceiling effect. The preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics validly measures whether a verifier detects faults in the identical candidate. Observing zero baseline faults yields a scientifically informative null/ceiling outcome: for this model, prompt/template, and task bank the generator outputs were uniformly valid on the emulated tasks, and the verifier produced no additional prevention. This outcome does not imply that verifiers are unnecessary in general; rather it highlights that verifier utility is conditional on generator error prevalence and on the choice of evaluation design.

Design implications for future GVR evaluations. (1) Shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate verifier detection on identical outputs but do not capture verifier value that arises via repairs or alternate generations; to measure repair‑mediated benefits, the experimental contract must permit repair calls and record repaired candidate outcomes. (2) Independent per‑condition generation arms (separate generation calls for baseline and guarded) or multi‑sample generation per task increase generator variability and therefore the probability of observing generator errors; they better test verifier detection and the end‑to‑end benefit of blocking faulty candidates. (3) Adversarial/fault‑injection task sets that intentionally increase semantic and ordering difficulty can produce non‑degenerate error regimes where verifier detection and false‑positive tradeoffs become measurable.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: one shared generation per intent and no model sampling parameters fixed in the run artifact (temperature = null in execution/model_configuration.json) means provider default sampling semantics governed generation; this residual sampling‑parameter uncertainty is archived and acknowledged. Construct validity: our outcome (emulator‑observed faults) is a conservative proxy for operational harm but may not cover higher‑level, temporal, or traffic‑dependent failures present in production. External validity: the experiment used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic/emulated topologies and therefore does not generalize across models, vendor dialects, or production devices. Conclusion validity: with zero baseline failures the confirmatory power to detect a verifier benefit is nil (ceiling effect); the registered power analysis target assumed a nonzero baseline error rate (target absolute paired reduction 0.20).

Operational implications and responsible interpretation. The observed absence of baseline faults in this controlled corpus suggests that, under constrained prompts, dialects, and emulation, modern LLMs can produce high task accuracy. However, this result should not be interpreted as evidence of production safety without broader stress testing, varied sampling, adversarial inputs, multi‑model comparisons, and human oversight in live environments.

Reproducibility: artifacts and deterministic accounting. All raw_results.jsonl, analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, missingness_summary.csv), scoring traces, execution manifest, deterministic_reconciliation.json, and model_configuration.json are archived and hashed in the evidence bundle. Representative artifact filenames and analysis artifact paths are provided in the evidence manifest (execution/* and analysis/*). The analysis bootstrap used seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples; these values are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Reproduction steps: (1) consult the execution manifest and model_configuration.json for declared model and adapter; (2) inspect execution/responses and execution/scoring artifacts for per‑task traces; (3) run the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1 script with the recorded input_results_sha256 to reproduce the contingency and inference outputs. (The full archived bundle contains these deterministic artifacts and hashes.)
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered, deterministic paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics (72 confirmatory pairs) to measure whether a canonical deterministic verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated configurations that would execute with operational faults. For the chosen model (gpt-5-mini), verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and task bank, baseline executions produced zero emulator‑observed faults; consequently the verifier did not change outcomes (paired difference 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0], exact McNemar p = 1.0). The principal, evidence‑grounded conclusion is conditional: verifier benefit depends on generator error prevalence and task realism. Confirmatory measurement of verifier utility under realistic error regimes requires experimental designs that (a) allow independent or multiple stochastic generations per condition, (b) include adversarial/fault‑injection tasks, and (c) compare across multiple models and sampling settings. We release deterministic execution manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support replication and follow‑on studies.

References

[1] N. Tu, S. Nam, J. W.‑K. Hong, "Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using Large Language Models," Network and Emerging Markets (Nem), 2024.
[2] Z. Wang et al., "Intent‑Driven Network Management with Multi‑Agent LLMs: The Confucius Framework," Proc. of the ACM Symp., 2025.
[3] R. Cadenas, "Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments," SSRN, 2026.
[4] P. Kazemian, M. T. Chang, H. Zeng, G. Varghese, N. McKeown, S. Whyte, "Real time network policy checking using header space analysis," 2013.

limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation, multi‑sample generation, or repairs unless explicitly permitted by the contract.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: execution/model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null indicates provider default sampling semantics determined runtime sampling behavior and is a residual uncertainty recorded in the archived configuration.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
